On Tuesday, March 31, 2020 at 7:41:34 AM UTC+11, Ken Kellner wrote:
> Hi,
>
> If I am understanding your question correctly, a potential alternative approach would be to use the empirical Bayes posterior predictive distribution. For some discussion see here:
>
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/qViR90-RHX4
>
> I wrote up a quick example based on the `colext` frog example below. In the future some of the functions I used will be built-in to unmarked (they already are in the dev version).
>
> library(unmarked)
>
> data(frogs)
> umf <- formatMult(masspcru)
> obsCovs(umf) <- scale(obsCovs(umf))
>
> ## Use 1/4 of data just for run speed in example
> umf <- umf[which((1:numSites(umf)) %% 4 == 0),]
>
> #Add fake site covariate as an example
> #takes values 'a' or 'b'
> siteCovs(umf) <- data.frame(fakeCov=factor(sample(c('a','b'), numSites(umf),
>                                     replace=T)))
> fm <- colext(psiformula = ~ fakeCov,
>              gammaformula = ~ fakeCov,
>              epsilonformula = ~ fakeCov,
>              pformula = ~ JulianDate + I(JulianDate^2), umf)
>
> # Empirical Bayes estimates of number of sites occupied in each year
> re <- ranef(fm)
>
> ########################################################################
> #These two functions below will be built-in in next version of unmarked
> #Sample from posterior
> postSamples <- function(object, nsims=100){
>
>   N <- dim(object@post)[1]
>   K <- dim(object@post)[2]
>   T <- dim(object@post)[3]
>
>   out <- array(NA, c(N, T, nsims))
>
>   for (n in 1:N){
>     for (t in 1:T){
>         out[n, t, ] <- sample(0:(K-1), nsims, replace=TRUE,
>                               prob=object@post[n,,t])
>     }
>   }
>   out
> }
>
> #predict method for ranef
> prRanef <- function(object, func, nsims=100){
>
>   ps <- postSamples(object, nsims=nsims)
>   s1 <- func(ps[,,1])
>   nm <- names(s1)
>   row_nm <- rownames(s1)
>   col_nm <- colnames(s1)
>
>   if(is.vector(s1)){
>     out_dim <- c(length(s1), nsims)
>   } else{
>     out_dim <- c(dim(s1), nsims)
>   }
>
>   param <- apply(ps, 3, func)
>
>   out <- array(param, out_dim)
>
>   if(is.vector(s1)){
>     rownames(out) <- nm
>   } else {
>     rownames(out) <- row_nm
>     colnames(out) <- col_nm
>   }
>
>   drop(out)
> }
> ###############################################################################
>
> #Custom function to calculate mean occupancy for each group fakeCov='a' or 'b'
> #in each time step, for a particular sample from posterior pred distribution
> avgOcc <- function(x){ #x takes as input M x T matrix (M sites, T years)
>
>   nyr <- umf@numPrimary
>   #output is matrix: 2x7, 2 groups (a and b), 7 years
>   out <- matrix(NA, nrow=2, ncol=nyr)
>   colnames(out) <- paste0('yr',1:nyr)
>   rownames(out) <- c('fakeCovA', 'fakeCovB')
>
>   #For each year, calculate the mean occupancy for each of the 2 groups
>   for (t in 1:nyr){
>     out[1,t] <- mean(x[siteCovs(umf)$fakeCov=='a',t])
>     out[2,t] <- mean(x[siteCovs(umf)$fakeCov=='b',t])
>   }
>
>   out
>
> }
>
> #Take 100 samples from posterior predictive distribution
> #and apply the function each sample
> set.seed(123)
> pr <- prRanef(re, func=avgOcc, nsims=100)
>
> #Output is 2x7x100
> pr
>
> #Mean occupancy for each treatment group for each time period
> apply(pr, c(1,2), mean)
>
> #Distribution of values for treatment a in year 1
> hist(pr[1,1,])
>
> #Fancy plot of mean occupancy for each treatment over time
> library(tidyverse)
> library(ggplot2)
>
> #Calculate means and 95% CI lower and upper bounds and tidy
> mns <- data.frame(apply(pr, c(1,2), mean)) %>%
>   rownames_to_column('treatment') %>%
>   gather(key='year',value='occ', yr1:yr7)
>
> lower <- data.frame(apply(pr, c(1,2), quantile, 0.025)) %>%
>   rownames_to_column('treatment') %>%
>   gather(key='year',value='lower', yr1:yr7)
>
> upper <- data.frame(apply(pr, c(1,2), quantile, 0.975)) %>%
>   rownames_to_column('treatment') %>%
>   gather(key='year',value='upper', yr1:yr7)
>
> plot_dat <- mns %>% left_join(lower) %>% left_join(upper)
>
> plot_dat %>%
>   mutate(year = as.numeric(gsub("yr", "", year))) %>% #convert yr to numeric
>   ggplot(aes(x=year, y=occ)) +
>   geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lower, ymax=upper,fill=treatment),alpha=0.4) +
>   geom_line(aes(col=treatment)) +
>   geom_point(aes(col=treatment), size=2) +
>   labs(x='Year',y='Mean occupancy') +
>   theme_bw() +
>   theme(panel.grid.major=element_blank(), panel.grid.minor=element_blank())
>
>
>
>

messages.subject_clean: How to check if positive or negative impact of chosen covariate
messages.body_plain:
Hello! A quick, basic question: I want to know if a specific covariate in a model is influencing the detectability/recruitment/survival in a negative or positive way. For example, I have this model:

om8_yellow <- pcountOpen(~1, ~Meadow, ~Reed, ~Day, data = umf_yellow, mixture = "ZIP", K = 2000, dynamics = "autoreg", fix = "none", se = TRUE)

where "day" is the day in the season (1, 2, 3...), "Meadow" is the proportion of meadow at the survey sites, and "Reed" is the proportion of reed at the survey sites. I want to know if detectability increases or decreases as the season progresses, if recruitment increases or decreases with a higher proportion of meadow, and if survival increases or decreases with a higher proportion of reed.

I ran summary(om8_yellow) and this is what I got:

Abundance (log-scale):

 Estimate    SE    z  P(>|z|)

     1.33 0.184 7.21 5.49e-13

Recruitment (log-scale):

            Estimate    SE      z P(>|z|)

(Intercept)   -0.173 0.227 -0.764  0.4451

Meadow         0.489 0.214  2.284  0.0224

Apparent Survival (logit-scale):

            Estimate   SE     z P(>|z|)

(Intercept)    -1.61 1.31 -1.23   0.219

Reed            7.87 7.53  1.05   0.296

Detection (logit-scale):

            Estimate      SE     z  P(>|z|)

(Intercept)   -1.102 0.26910 -4.09 4.24e-05

Day           -0.056 0.00786 -7.13 1.01e-12

Zero-inflation (logit-scale):

 Estimate   SE      z P(>|z|)
    -9.93 36.4 -0.273   0.785

Should I look at the "Estimate" for each and interpret positive numbers as there is a positive effect and vice versa for negative number?  So for example in this case, a higher proportion of meadow gives higher recruitment, a higher proportion of reed gives higher survival, and the detectability decreases as the season progresses? Thank you in advance.

messages.body_plain:
Hello unmarked community,

I´m totally new to distance sampling models but I have this amazing data from a bird monitoring program I´d like to use to understand more about the ecology of forest birds. I hope you can help me clarifying two very basic questions. First, the description of the data set
243  3-km linear transects divided into six 500m-sections
abundance recorded along 3 distance bands: 0-25, 25-100, 100-1000m
4 surveys a year (2 breeding season, 2 winter season). I´m just interested in breeding season so I was planning to use the max. value over the two breeding surveys for each transect-section.
data collected over the period 2006-2011
I want to understand spatial variation of abundances over forested landscapes. However, my forest structure data is one for the whole period (i.e. there is not yearly variation). I´m not interested in the annual variation of abundance (so I´m not sure I need to estimate availability 'phi'  on a yearly basis; gdistsamp function, temporary emigration model Chandler et al. 2011). I  just would like to squeeze the most of the data I have for the period the forest structure data was built.

I´ve looked through other questions in this group and I found something similar from 2016!
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/DvliCEn91BI
where Andy recommended using the gdistsamp function with 'stacked' data structure. I think this will work for my case too but...

My questions here are,
how should I deal with yearly 'pseudoreplication'? (would adding a factor(year) as a predictor among the abundance covariates suffice?)
would it make sense at all to use all the abundance data for the 6 years (2006-2011) when I only have one estimate of forest landscape and structure for the whole period?
how could I incorporate in the model the potential autocorrelation between abundance values along the six sections of each linear transect? (I understand the model does not accept a random effect for the transect. I guess I could add the transect as a fixed effect but it has 243 levels!). Is looking for autocorrelation in residuals the only thing I can do?
Many thanks for your reading until here and your help
Best,
Ale

messages.body_plain:
Alejandra,

First, I wouldn't dismiss the temporary emigration model.  I think your approach is fine, but you may be more fully taking advantage of your two surveys with gmultmix.

Your question on stacking data has been covered a lot in this group.  Last I read, it appeared to be generally acceptable as long as you used the year covariate.

To account for spatial autocorrelation, one approach is to add a covariate for densities in adjacent transects or sections (i.e. autologistic regression); see here for more direction: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/unmarked/KYrrgnxVzAg/Srm9UqXkz3QJ.

Regarding using one measure of forest structure, 6 years seems like a long time--you'd need to assume that there was no significant disturbance or succession or management. Repeat structure measures from a subset of transects would be useful.  But with the size of your dataset, I wonder if it's necessary to push that assumption, as you'd have good numbers for many bird species in even a single year.  Estimating spatial and temporal trends using data across the full timeframe, regardless of structure/landscape variables, would likely be useful.

-Mike Worland

Hello unmarked community,

I'm starting with occupancy / abundance modeling and I have some questions about my data:

I have tried to understand the occupancy of giant anteater in a protected area. I modeled the single species single season occupancy with occu function at unmarked. The problem is that my models doesn't have a good fit (I do the GoF at modavg), all of them results in a high overdispersion (SE = NaN).
I think the sample size is too small (58 sites x 45 occasions) for the number of covariables I have (9 covariable site and 2 obs covariable).

There is some other occupancy model that my data fitted better?

Am I doing something wrong?

Yes - negative AIC values are legitimate and interpreted in the same way as positive AIC values. The negative AIC arises due to the portion of the multinomial coefficient that is computed. Frequently, for computational efficiency, terms are dropped from the likelihood expression that are not functions of the parameters of interest (usually ugly factyorial terms). Hi Jessica,
I think it is because you forgot the occuMulti sintaxis, that is a little bit different from occ.

When you fit an occuMulti model you must add the psi (occformulas) and p (detformulas) formulas, which are vectors of what you wish to model.
The det formulas must be a vector equal to your species number in this case 2: c("~1","~1"), here we state that no covs affect the anteater and doc detections.
On the other hand occ formulas object is  a vector of the same length as your umf@fDesing (this calls your design matrix) columns, in this case three: 1. Anteater psi, 2. Dog psi and Anteater|dog psi. You can express it like this c("~1", "~1", "~1") in the case you want to model the conditional occupancy.

So you can try this

null <- occuMulti(c("~1","~1"), c("~1", "~1", "0"), umf ) # model without interactions or covs

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicholas,

There's no straightforward way to do what you are asking in unmarked. If you provide multiple factor levels in the newdata as you have done in your example, you will get one predicted value for each of these factor levels. These predictions will have the same value for x (elevation) but different values of y, which leads to the ugly plot you are seeing.

Usually for a plot like the one you are making, focused on one continuous covariate, I would just use the baseline/reference levels of each categorical covariate, or plot multiple lines on each plot with each line corresponding to a different factor level. It doesn't really make sense to me conceptually to try to get the "mean" of a categorical variable. If you have elevation measurements of 0 and 100, the mean=50 is generally a possible observed value in the dataset. But "averaging" across land covers is creating a new "category" that doesn't exist in reality.

If you really want this I suppose you could get predicted values for your range of elevations at each individual land cover level, one at a time, and then calculate an average value across all land covers for each elevation value in your sequence.

Ken

Hi Nick,

Not exactly an answer to the question you're asking, but I think this might help. If you're interested in seeing the effect of elevation on PSI in the different land cover types you could visualize that by modifying how you're plotting the predicted dataframe (of course this will be the same slope without an interaction term, but as a place to start) . Try plotting with ggplot and use facet_wrap(~lctype). That will give you 7 different panels, with PSI on the y axis, and elevation of the x. If you're not familiar with ggplot that code might look something like this for you:

#make your predicted dataframe
pred_data<-predict(mod2, type="state", newdata=newdata, appendData=TRUE)

#plot it
ggplot(pred_data , aes(elevation,Predicted))+
geom_line()+
geom_ribbon(aes(ymin =lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.3)+
ylab(expression(italic(psi)))+
xlab(elevation)+
facet_wrap(~lctype)

Hope this helps.
Kevin

Hello dear all, I am trying to estimate the adult sex ratio using distance sampling data. For that, I 've modified the code proposer by Ancona et al. 2017 which is also based in a code proposed in Ch6 of the AHM book. This code was initially written to capture and recapture data, so I 've considered that as a site as each stop that we have done to count and identify animals. Since at each stop, there are adults that are sexed and adults that are not sexed,  there is a probability to identify sex. In my model species, there is no sexual dimorphism, so chances to identify an adult male or female are the same. To do that you need to observe the testes or the vulva.
When I run the code, I get this warning:

Warning message:
In sqrt(diag(v)) : NaNs produced

I have read in this group that this might be due to sparse data or small data sets can cause this warning, and a smaller model should be written for this data. But in my case I can't think of a smaller model and I am not sure if calculating sex proportion without tacking account that there is a probability of not identifying sex is a good choice. Any help is really welcome. I paste my code below and attach a data file in case some is interested in have a look to my data.

data10<-read.csv(file="feb2010.csv",header=TRUE,sep=",",dec=".")
males10<-matrix(data10$machos.id <http://machos.id>)
females10<-matrix(data10$hembras.id <http://hembras.id>)
males10_na<-na.omit(males10)
females10_na<-na.omit(females10)
sex_prop_trad10<-sum(males10_na)/(sum(males10_na)+sum(females10_na)) #traditional estimation of sex proportions
sex_prop_trad10
library(unmarked)
#males
umf1 <- unmarkedFramePCount(y = males10_na)   # Create unmarked data frame for males
summary(umf1)                             # Summarize
na.omit(umf1)
(fm1 <- pcount(~1 ~1, data = umf1))       # Fit model: get estimates on link scale
backTransform(fm1, "state")               # Get estimates on natural scale
backTransform(fm1, "det")

mean_Nmales <-  backTransform(fm1, "state")@estimate  # mean estimated abundance

#females
umf2 <- unmarkedFramePCount(y = females10_na)  # Create unmarked data frame for females
na.omit(umf2)
summary(umf2)                       # Summarize
(fm2 <- pcount(~1 ~1, data = umf2)) # Fit model: get estimates on link scale
backTransform(fm2, "state")         # Get estimates on natural scale
backTransform(fm2, "det")

mean_Nfemales <-  backTransform(fm2, "state")@estimate  # mean estimated abundance

est_males_scn1 <- bup(ranef(fm1))
est_females_scn1 <- bup(ranef(fm2))

cbind(males=est_males_scn1,females=est_females_scn1,estimated_SR=round(random_est_SR_scn1,2))

(cbind(males=mean_Nmales,females=mean_Nfemales,estimated_SR=round(SR_1,2)))

Antonela

messages.subject_clean: Tricky dataset & whether pcountOpen is appropriate framework
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am currently working with a bit of a tricky dataset and am wondering more broadly if the open population N-mixture approach (i.e. Dail & Madsen 2011) is the right way to go. I have a lot of experience with occupancy models, but this is my first foray into the N-mixture world.

The dataset comprises three years of nightly acoustic recordings of bats outside a hibernaculum during spring emergence. There are 12 detectors, and the first "hump" of bat calls during emergence takes place over ~12 nights in each year. The goal of this project is to answer "What habitat features are bats using as they emerge from the hibernaculum?" (and, more broadly, how can this information to be used to assist recovery from white-nose syndrome).

The number of bats on the landscape changes daily -- bats emerge from the hibernaculum, use the immediate landscape around the hibernaculum (where the detector array is located), and then disperse to maternity colonies -- so this is clearly an open population. Detection will vary by temperature and, to a lesser extent, other weather-related variables such as relative humidity, wind speed, precipitation, etc. I was planning to apply pcountOpen to each year separately, using 12 replicates (nightly counts over 12 nights) at 12 sites (detectors). I know our sample size is low.

My two questions are:

(1) Will modeling covariates on gamma (ie "immigration," the number of bats entering the landscape daily) be the key to answering our question about what habitat features bats are using? I was thinking (as the number of calls is hump-shaped over time) gamma could be modeled as

julianday + julianday^2 + lidarmeasure1 + lidarmeasure2 + ....

(2) Double-counting of bats is almost certain due to the detectors recording all night long & an inability to identify individual bats on the detectors. I know this is a major assumption of N-mixture models and that traditional GOF models will fail to pick up on even the slightest of violations. A counterargument from my collaborators is that bias on N doesn't matter, as we aren't interested in abundance estimation but rather use of habitat features by incoming bats. How slippery is this slope?

Any advice appreciated from those with more experience with this class of models. My thanks in advance for your time and attention.

Best,
Lisanne
